scenes.dialogue: A news report says police custody. Another says judicial custody. Do both mean the same thing? Who controls the person, and for how long?
Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, or B N S S, these are different forms of detention, with important safeguards.
scenes.shown: Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, or BNSS, these are different forms of detention, with important safeguards.

scenes.dialogue: Start with an arrest without warrant. Section Fifty Eight prohibits detention beyond twenty four hours without a Magistrate's authorisation.
scenes.shown: Start with an arrest without warrant. Section 58 prohibits detention beyond 24 hours without a Magistrate's authorisation.

scenes.dialogue: Necessary travel time to court is excluded, and police must avoid unnecessary delay.
Suppose Ravi is arrested on Monday morning. Officers cannot keep him at the station for days because questioning is unfinished.
If further detention is needed, Section One Eighty Seven requires production before a Magistrate.
scenes.shown: If further detention is needed, Section 187 requires production before a Magistrate.

scenes.dialogue: The Magistrate must then consider whether remand is justified.
In police custody, the accused is entrusted to investigating police for lawful investigation under the remand order.
That can include lawful questioning, or recovering evidence.
In judicial custody, the accused is ordinarily kept in prison under jail authorities, pursuant to the court's order.
The investigating officer does not have the same direct custody.
Both forms require legal justification. Neither is a finding of guilt, and judicial custody does not mean a conviction.
Here is the key limit under the ordinary B N S S scheme.
scenes.shown: Here is the key limit under the ordinary BNSS scheme.

scenes.dialogue: Section One Eighty Seven, sub section Two, as the Supreme Court reads it, allows fifteen days of police custody in all.
scenes.shown: Section 187(2), as the Supreme Court reads it, allows 15 days of police custody in all.

scenes.dialogue: Together or in parts, those days must fall within the first forty days of remand in a sixty day case, or the first sixty in a ninety day case.
scenes.shown: Together or in parts, those days must fall within the first 40 days of remand in a 60-day case, or the first 60 in a 90-day case.

scenes.dialogue: Forty and sixty describe the window, not the number of days police may keep someone.
The Supreme Court confirmed this in July twenty twenty six. Every grant still needs the Magistrate's decision.
scenes.shown: The Supreme Court confirmed this in July 2026. Every grant still needs the Magistrate's decision.

scenes.dialogue: Assume Ravi's case is in the sixty day category, and he stays in custody throughout. The Magistrate grants five days of police custody.
scenes.shown: Assume Ravi's case is in the 60-day category, and he stays in custody throughout. The Magistrate grants five days of police custody.

scenes.dialogue: Then judicial custody follows, and new evidence emerges in the investigation.
On day twenty, police ask for another five days of police custody.
scenes.shown: On day 20, police ask for another five days of police custody.

scenes.dialogue: The Magistrate may grant them if justified, because all five days fall within the first forty days, and only ten of the fifteen would be used.
scenes.shown: The Magistrate may grant them if justified, because all five days fall within the first 40 days, and only ten of the fifteen would be used.

scenes.dialogue: Returning to police custody does not create a fresh fifteen day allowance, or restart the overall remand clock.
scenes.shown: Returning to police custody does not create a fresh 15-day allowance, or restart the overall remand clock.

scenes.dialogue: Section One Eighty Seven, sub section Four, requires physical production before the Magistrate for every police remand.
scenes.shown: Section 187(4) requires physical production before the Magistrate for every police remand.

scenes.dialogue: Judicial custody may be extended through physical or audio video production.
scenes.shown: Judicial custody may be extended through physical or audio-video production.

scenes.dialogue: Under sub section Seven, the Magistrate must record reasons for police custody. A police request is not a remand order.
scenes.shown: Under sub-section (7), the Magistrate must record reasons for police custody. A police request is not a remand order.

scenes.dialogue: To move Ravi from prison into police custody, investigators need a fresh court order within the limits.
Section One Eighty Seven, sub section Three, sets the investigation detention periods linked to default bail.
scenes.shown: Section 187(3) sets the investigation detention periods linked to default bail.

scenes.dialogue: It specifies ninety days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment for ten years or more.
scenes.shown: It specifies 90 days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment for 10 years or more.

scenes.dialogue: And sixty days for other offences. The exact charge, and the applicable judicial interpretation, matter.
scenes.shown: And 60 days for other offences. The exact charge, and the applicable judicial interpretation, matter.

scenes.dialogue: Police and judicial custody both count towards the applicable total. It is not fifteen days plus another sixty or ninety.
scenes.shown: Police and judicial custody both count towards the applicable total. It is not 15 days plus another 60 or 90.

scenes.dialogue: Special laws can modify these rules, so the ordinary figures cannot be applied blindly.
Expiry alone does not open the prison gates. If the required charge sheet is missing, the accused must claim default bail in time.
He must also be ready to furnish bail. A timely charge sheet can let judicial custody continue through lawful orders.
After cognizance or the start of trial, Section Three Forty Six permits remand when proceedings are postponed or adjourned.
scenes.shown: After cognizance or the start of trial, Section 346 permits remand when proceedings are postponed or adjourned.

scenes.dialogue: That is a maximum of fifteen days at a time under that section, which is different from the fifteen day police custody limit.
scenes.shown: That is a maximum of 15 days at a time under that section, which is different from the 15-day police custody limit.

scenes.dialogue: Custody does not remove basic rights. Section Forty Seven requires the grounds of arrest to be communicated forthwith.
scenes.shown: Custody does not remove basic rights. Section 47 requires the grounds of arrest to be communicated forthwith.

scenes.dialogue: Section Forty Eight requires informing a nominated relative or friend.
scenes.shown: Section 48 requires informing a nominated relative or friend.

scenes.dialogue: Section Thirty Eight gives the right to meet an advocate during interrogation, though not throughout it.
scenes.shown: Section 38 gives the right to meet an advocate during interrogation, though not throughout it.

scenes.dialogue: Sections Fifty Three and Fifty Six provide for medical examination, and for the health and safety of the arrested person.
scenes.shown: Sections 53 and 56 provide for medical examination, and for the health and safety of the arrested person.

scenes.dialogue: And bail can be sought before the maximum custody periods expire; the court need not use every available day.
Police custody places the accused with investigators, for authorised investigation.
Judicial custody ordinarily places the accused in prison, under court orders.
Remember the ordinary limits: twenty four hours before a Magistrate must authorise detention, and fifteen police custody days in all.
scenes.shown: Remember the ordinary limits: 24 hours before a Magistrate must authorise detention, and 15 police-custody days in all.

scenes.dialogue: All of it sits inside the forty, sixty and ninety day framework.
scenes.shown: All of it sits inside the 40, 60 and 90-day framework.
